full_judgment:
These four Matters permit of analogous hearing because of commonality of factual background and issues raised and are, therefore, disposed of accordingly.

Company Matter No. 88 of 2006

2. On 21-5-2006, the instant Company Matter was filed by the Petitioner, Mr Shamsul Alain Bhuiyan ("SAB"), under section 43 of the Companies Act 1994 (the "CA 1994"). The Respondent No. 1 is the Registrar of Joint Stock Companies and Firms ("RJSC"), the Respondent No. 2 is the City Bank Ltd. ("CBL"), the Respondent No. 3 is Ahmed Iqbal Hasan & Co. ("Hasan & Co."), the Respondent No. 4 is Bangladesh Finance & Investment Co. Ltd ("BFIC"), the Respondent No. 5 is the Bangladesh Securities & Exchange Commission ("SEC"), the Respondent No. 6 is the Dhaka Stock Exchange ("DSE"), the Respondent No. 7 is Saber Ahmed Chowdhury ("SAC") and the Respondent No. 8 is Zakir Hossain ("ZH").

3. In his section 43 application, SAB initially sought certain orders from this Court, which included the following:

(i) To direct the Respondent No. 3, Ahmed Iqbal Hasan and Co. ("Hasan & Co."), to 	hand over the share certificates of 38,400 ordinary shares (the "Disputed Shares") of the 	Respondent No. 2, the City Bank Limited ("CBL") to SAB;

(ii) To direct the Respondent No.4, Bangladesh Finance and Investment Co. Ltd, ("BFIC"), to issue a No-Objection Certificate in respect of the Disputed Shares to be transferred in the name of SAB; and

(iii) Pending hearing of the section 43 application a direction on CBL that it should not enter the name of any other person or persons in the place of SAB in its share register and Hasan & Co. not to sell or transfer the Disputed Shares.

4. On 18-5-2010, SAB amended the prayer of his section 43 application, with the leave of this Court, and prayed for an order so that CBL is directed to rectify its share register and enter the name of SAB as the owner of the Disputed Shares as well as the related rights and bonus shares issued against the same.

5. The relevant factual background, in short and as alleged by SAB, is that ZH took a loan (the "First Loan") from BFIC. In this connection, SAC pledged, as third party security for the First Loan, the Disputed Shares to BFIC. SAC delivered the signed share transfer forms relating to the Disputed Shares to BFIC in order to perfect the pledge. On 14-3-2002, BFIC acted upon the pledge and, without informing ZH or SAC, transferred the Disputed Shares in its own name. In the meantime, on 8-10-2002, ZH repaid the First Loan. SAB claims that after ZH fully adjusted the First Loan from BFIC, SAC entered into an understanding with SAB, on 26-12-2002, and transferred the Disputed Shares along with 19,200 right shares (the "Rights Shares") to SAB.

6. On 29-12-2002, SAB took a loan of Taka 68,00,000 (the "Second Loan") from BFIC keeping as security 31,130 ordinary shares of CBL along with the Disputed Shares. On 30-11-2003, SAB partially paid the Second Loan and was returned the 31,130 ordinary shares by BFIC while the Disputed Shares were still kept as security. After partly adjusting the Second Loan, SAB allegedly entered into an understanding with Hasan & Co. subsequently that it would fully adjust the remaining Second Loan and release the Disputed Shares from BFIC. Hasan & Co. would then sell the Disputed Shares and give the sale proceeds to SAB, after deducting its commission.

7. On 18-4-2004, Hasan & Co. fully adjusted the Second Loan taken by SAB and received possession of the Disputed Shares. In this connection, on 20-4-2004, SAB allegedly gave 2 (two) blank share transfer forms to Hasan & Co. to sell the Disputed Shares through the DSE. Since the Disputed Shares were being held in the name of BFIC, SAB wrote a letter on 21-7-2004 and requested BFIC to issue a No Objection Certificate in order to complete the transfer of the Disputed Shares. But, SAB did not receive any reply from BFIC.

8. It is alleged that Hasan & Co. after obtaining the Disputed Shares did not sell the same through the DSE when the share price was high. This is so despite several reminders by SAB. As a result, Hasan & Co. acted irresponsibly and without exercising its due skills. Accordingly, a legal notice was sent on 15-12k 2004 by SAB. But, no reply was received from Hasan & Co. On 16-3-2005, SAB also wrote and complained to the SEC and DSE in this regard.

9. SAB's main allegation against BFIC is that it intentionally and with fraudulent intent held the Disputed Shares in its own name even after receiving the requisite price for the same and that Hasan & Co. is not giving the due account of the Disputed Shares despite receiving several reminders from SAB. It is alleged that, at all material times, Hasan & Co. and BFIC have denied SAB's title to the Disputed Shares.

10. SAB would like the Disputed Shares back from Hasan & Co. on payment of the amount that Hasan & Co. had paid to BFIC. Being aggrieved by this, SAB filed the section 43 application and prayed for the relief against BFIC and Hasan & Co.

11. Thereafter, several Supplementary Affidavits were filed, from time to time, by SAB adducing evidence supporting, inter alia, SAB's claims against BFIC and Hasan & Co. On one occasion, SAB (relying on newspaper cuttings) alleged that Hasan & Co., after obtaining the Disputed Shares from BFIC, transferred those to Latif Securities Ltd., who then sold the same to Mr Mussadeque Ali Falu and his wife Ms. Nadia Ali. In search of the Disputed Shares, SAB also wrote a letter to CBL, on 3-11-2010, and requested it to provide/disclose any movement relating to the Disputed Shares since February 2002. CBL replied to SAB's letter on 27-12.2010, and clearly informed SAB that the, Disputed Shares were transferred to BFIC on 14-3-2002, which was subsequently transferred to Capital Market Services Limited on 16-6- 2004. The Disputed Shares were ultimately transferred to various third parties.

12. On the other hand, CBL filed an Affidavit-in-Opposition clearly stating that SAB was never the owner of the Disputed Shares as per its records. This was the position of CBL since the inception of the instant matter and is corroborated further by CBL's letter dated 27 June 2005 (Annexure-J of section 43 application annexed by SAB) to the SEC, which clearly stated that SAB was never the owner of the Disputed Shares. As per CBL's records, the Disputed Shares were transferred from SAC to BFIC on 14-3-2002. On 16-6-2004, the Disputed Shares were transferred from BFIC to Capital Market Services Limited. Thereafter, the Disputed Shares were transferred to bonafide third party purchasers, all before the filing of the instant section 43 application. CBL also stated that, at the time of these transfers, SAB never even complained and/or objected to CBL regarding the transfer of the Disputed Shares.

13. Hasan & Co. also filed an Affidavit-in-Opposition clearly stating that SAB was never the owner of the Disputed Shares as per its records. Hasan & Co. stated that SAC never admitted that he assigned his interest in the Disputed Shares to SAB. In this connection, SAC never submitted any documents relating to such assignment of interest. Hasan & Co. also questioned the validity of the documents submitted by SAB and stated, with explanation, that the documents are fictitious. It stated that the Share Sale Agreement (Annexure A of the section 43 application) between SAC and BFIC was entered into on 27-1-2002 but it referred to future events, which raises serious doubts as to its authenticity. Hasan & Co. also stated that it is not factually possible to assign the Disputed Shares to SAB if they were pledged to and under the custody of BFIC. Also, Hasan & Co. stated that the Disputed Shares were not clearly identified in the Share Sale Agreement (Annexure A of the section 43 application).

14. Hasan & Co. also stated that, on SAB's own admission, the Disputed Shares were in the custody of BFIC along with share transfer forms issued by SAC. Therefore, it is not possible for SAC to enter into any lawful transaction with any person, including SAB, with regard to the Disputed Shares without first releasing the Disputed Shares from BFIC. Hasan & Co. submitted that it is both factually and legally impossible that SAC had transferred his ownership of the Disputed Shares and any related rights shares to SAB. It also begs the question that whether SAC had entered into various arrangements with different persons with regards to the same set of Disputed Shares for his own financial gain, attracting criminal liability for fraudulent acts. Hasan & Co. stated that SAB did not also submit any documents which would prove that there was an understanding between SAC, SAB and BFIC to deposit any money to CBL. As a result, the story of SAB and SAC entering into any form of "understanding" to transfer the Disputed Shares to SAB is fictitious and false. Hasan & Co. also submitted that as the Disputed Shares were already pledged to BFIC for the First Loan, the same could not have been pledged in order to obtain the Second Loan by SAB. Hence, the contention of SAB is not only incorrect but also fabricated.

15. Ms Tania Amir appearing for the Respondent No. 3 Hasan & Co. has forcefully argued on the case of "elusive understandings" as above noted. She has argued that BFIC loans obtained by repeatedly assigning "interests" in the same set of shares speaks of a "scam" and that the Petitioner in this instance is seen to be leveraging on shares that had already previously been "pledged, sold and transferred."

16. Most importantly, contrary to SAB's allegations, it is clear that SAB was never known to Hasan & Co. and they had no transaction together. SAB lodged a complaint to DSE for investigating the irregularity in selling /transferring the Disputed Shares. Based on the complaint, on 22-5-2005 (Annexure-Y(1) of DSE's Affidavit-in-Opposition), the Investigation committee of DSE submitted an Inspection Report which runs follows:

"Report Summary

According to SEC letter reference No. SEC/SRMID/94-130/693, dated 7th May, 2005, DSE monitoring team inspected the said house and scrutinize the books of records regarding the' complain lodged by name (complainant). Subsequently monitoring team examined the house's activities and relevant records of Ahmed Iqbal Hasan & Co. The findings of which are furnished as under:

Findings:

a. Monitoring did not find any client  namely Mr Abu Taleb Chowc1hury, Mr  Abu, Hossain & Mr Shamsul Alam Bhuiyan mentioned in complaint letter send to us by Securities and Exchange  commission after examining the client account opening forms 	and client registrar of the said member house."

17. Therefore, it is submitted that it is not possible that Hasan & Co. had made any offer that it would pay off the balance of any loan taken by SAB and release the Disputed Shares from BFIC. SAB has failed to provide any evidence of any contract in this regard. It is denied that Hasan & Co. ever paid Taka 40,80,142 to BFIC and the cheque was never issued by Hasan & Co. since the signature is not the signature of the Managing Director of Hasan & Co. It is clear that Hasan & Co. never obtained the Disputed Shares as claimed by SAB. It admitted that it received a legal notice dated 15-12-2004 and replied to it on 25-2-2005 denying the contents of the same.

18. Lastly, Hasan & Co. further submitted that SAB has filed another Company Matter, being Company Matter No. 35 of 2015, where it is stated in paragraph 15 "That since the shares were still in the name of BFIC, therefore, Mr Hassan could not sell the shares through DSE unless the same is transferred to the Petitioner". Conversely, the prayer (B) of the instant section 43 application states as follows: "After hearing the parties pass an order directing the respondent No. 3 to hand over the said 38,400 share certificate (as described in paragraph 10 of the petition) to the Petitioner on payment of money to the respondent No. 3 which he paid to respondent No. 4". Thus, SAB's malafide intention is clear. Also, it is clear that SAB has unlawfully suppressed the material facts, which amount to deceiving this Court.

19. BFIC also filed an Affidavit-in-Opposition and in short, denied the allegations of SAB. BFIC initially stressed on the prayers sought by SAB. BFIC submitted that if rectification is allowed then there is no need for No-Objection Certificates (the "NOCs") from BFIC. Hence, there is no claim by SAB against BFIC.

20. BFIC stated that, contrary to SAB's allegations, it is untrue that there was any understanding on 26-12-2002 in respect of 19,200 right shares (arising out of the Disputed Shares) because those were not yet issued at that time since the deposit of the requisite money for the rights shares was required by 29-12-2002. It is further stated that BFIC is unaware of any understanding between itself being on one side, and SAC and SAB being on other side regarding the deposit of money for the 19,200 rights shares, or for transfer of the same to SAB. The right shares were issued to BFIC on payment of requisite money on 26-12-2002 because it was the owner of the Disputed Shares on that date. CBL's affidavit supported this, as it states that the Disputed Shares were held in BFIC's name since 14-3-2002. Accordingly, the right shares were issued on 30-12-2002 to BFIC.

21. Moreover, BFIC referred to SAB's letter dated 29-7-2004 (Annexure-F of section 43 application) to BFIC wherein SAB clearly admitted that BFIC had handed over the signed share transfer instruments to SAB. Hence, if that is the case, there is no need to issue the NOCs as sought by SAB since SAB became entitled to register his name himself in the share register of CBL. As regards the Disputed Shares, BFIC stated that SAB enclosed a pay order bearing No. 08B 2106297 dated 18-4-2004 with a letter dated 15-4-2004 (Annexure-4 of BFIC's Affidavit-in-Opposition) for repayment of the principal amount of the Second Loan, along with a request for waiving interest, and instructions to return the Disputed Shares along with blank form 117s to one Mr Md Shafiqul Islam. BFIC did as requested on 19-4-2004 and received an acknowledgement receipt from Mr Shafiqul Islam (Annexure-5 of BFIC's Affidavit-in-Opposition). As a result, there is no need to issue the NOCs sought by SAB. Also, since the Disputed Shares were in the name of BFIC (after 14-3-2002), SAC could not have assigned the Disputed Shares to SAB.

22. Lastly, BFIC stressed that the 19,200 rights shares were issued on 30-12-2002, at the time when BFIC was the owner of the Disputed Shares. Therefore, BFIC was lawfully entitled to subscribe to those 19,200 rights shares. The Disputed Shares which were pledged were returned to SAB and this was acknowledged by SAB's nominated representative. In short, BFIC's case is that it was not holding any of the Disputed Shares as alleged by SAB. Hence, it is impossible for BFIC to have caused any loss to SAB. There is also no question of any fraud by BFIC against SAB as there is no share of SAB remaining with BFIC in view of the fact that the pledged Disputed Shares had been returned to SAB.

23. Importantly, DSE submitted an Affidavit-in-Opposition and stated that a complaint was lodged with the DSE, whereby SAB complained against Hasan & Co. and BFIC, requesting DSE to investigate the illegality committed by Hasan & Co. when selling the Disputed Shares. Accordingly, the DSE set up an inquiry committee which investigated this situation on 14-5-2005, and submitted the report to DSE on 22-5-2005 (Annexure-Y(1) of DSE's Affidavit-in-Opposition). The report was also sent to SEC on 4-6-2005. The report concluded that SAB, along with Petitioners in Company Matter Nos. 89 and 90 of 2006, were never the clients of Hasan & Co:

"Findings:

a. Monitoring team did not find any client namely Mr Abu Taleb Chowdhury, Mr  Abul 	Hossain, & Mr Shamsul Alam  Bhuiyan mentioned in complaint letter  send to us by 	Securities and Exchange commission after examining the client account opening forms 	and client registrar of the said member house.

b. Monitoring team did not find any evidence to support the claims that Taka 27,29,884 paid to BFIL through pay order # 08B 2106296 dated 18-4-2004 issued by Agrani Bank from this member houses funds.

c. Monitoring team did not find any record of regarding any transact of shares mentioned 	in the complaint letter through this Member house.

d. Monitoring team find out that the signature shown in the attach copies provided by the plaintiff is not similar to the signature of the complainant.

e. Monitoring team found that the account opening form sent by the plaintiff (that came to us through SEC) is not similar to the account opening form used by the said house. The signature duly signed in the account opening form is not the original signature of the member. Even the signature of the authorized person appears vague as it do not match with signature any of the authorized persons in the house.

Conclusion and remarks

According to the inspection in the said house regarding this issue, we may conclude that, the complaint 19dged by plaintiff is vague, ambiguous and without any proper evidence. We refer this for your kind acknowledgement."

24. CBL's legal Counsel Mr Sameer Sattar has at the outset critiqued the robust and "creative" devices resorted to by the learned Counsel for the Petitioner Mr Junayed Ahmed Chowdhury to raise very complicated disputed questions of fact. Mr Sattar emphasizes that in reality this case is a very simple one form the perspective of section 43. By Mr Sattar's reckoning much of SAB's case and Mr junayed Ahmed Chowdhury's extensive submissions and written memorial regarding privity with Hasan & Co. and the latter's liabilities under Securities Laws is liable to be ignored by this Court. This Court is inclined to do so finding merit in Mr Sattar's response as detailed herein below. But prior to that it is deemed prudent to take note of the following submissions in common advanced by the Petitioners in Matter Nos. 88, 89 and 90 of 2016:

(a) Hasan & Co., by paying off the Petitioners loans in BFIC, has violated section 16(a) of the Securities and Exchange Commission Ordinance 1969 ("the SEC Ordinance") and consequently, the transactions between the Petitioners and Hasan & Co. being a void transaction, the parties are liable to restore the benefits they had received thereunder as per section 65 of the Contract Act, 1872.

(b) If the transactions between the Petitioners and Hasan & Co. are not violative of section 16(a) of the SEC Ordinance, then Hasan & Co., in breach of its stock brokerage contract with the Petitioners, failed to sell the Shares in the floor of DSE and by 'handing over the Shares to Latif Securities, violated paragraph 2(1) of the Stock Brokers Code of 	Conduct listed in Second Schedule of Securities and Exchange Commission (Stock Dealer, Stock Broker and Authorised Representative) Rules 2000 ("The Stock Broker Rules") read with Rule 4(5) and 4A of the Securities and Exchange Rules 1987 ("the SEC Rules") and Regulation 42(1) of the Listing Regulations of DSE ("the DSE Listing Regulations").

(c) Hasan & Co., being the Petitioners' stock broker, violated section 17 of the SEC Ordinance and/or Rule 11 of the Stock Broker Rules read with paragraphs 1, 2, 3 and 7 of 	the Stock Brokers Code of Conduct.

(d) Latif Securities by entering into the transaction with Hasan & Co. has violated paragraph 8 of the Stock Brokers Code of Conduct.

25. Proceeding on the factual assumptions made by the Petitioners in all three Matter Nos. 88, 89 and 90 on the liability of Hasan & Co. the relief sought in common has been thus:

(a) Since the disputed Shares are not traceable in the hands of any particular individual(s) or the addresses of such individuals are unknown due to dematerialization, Hasan & Co., being in breach of its obligation under section 16(a) and 17 of the SEC Ordinance and paragraphs 1, 2(1), 3 and 7 of the Stock Brokers Code of Conduct and Rule 11 of the Stock Broker Rules read with Rule 4(5) and 4A of the SEC Rules and Regulation 42(1) of the DSE Listing Regulations shall be obligated to pay damages to the Petitioners in the amount of Taka 1,07,18,566 (under Matter No. 88), Taka 99,43,962 (under Matter No. 90) as restitutionary payment on account of the Disputed Shares.

(b) Since the bonus shares issued against the Disputed Shares are not traceable in the hands of any particular individual(s) or the addresses of such individuals are unknown due to dematerialization, CBL shall be obligated to pay damages to the Petitioners in the amount of Taka 13,81,84,049 (under Matter No. 88), Taka 9,35,61,427.7 (under Matter No. 89) and Taka 12,99,77,963.3 (under Matter No. 90) as payment for loss of opportunity on account of such bonus shares because CBL at all material times, is and was aware of the pendency of the litigation in the Company Matters and despite such knowledge of sub judice matters, CBL allowed issuance of bonus shares against the Shares in question.

26. It is here that Mr Sattar pertinently and appropriately sets the terms of reference under section 43 for this Court thus:

"This is not a case of violation of Securities Laws & Contractual Arrangements. Such issues cannot form a basis for a section 43 Application. Indeed, there are no ingredients in SAB's case for a section 43 Application".

27. Apart from the unclear factual events in relation to the handling and tracing of the Disputed Shares, as is evident from Hasan & Co., BFIC and DSE's Affidavit-in-Opposition, CBL's legal counsel, Md Sameer Sattar, submitted that the instant section 43 application is not legally maintainable. In this connection, Mr Sattar relied on various legal grounds. Firstly, CBL submitted that SAB had failed to satisfy the ingredients of section 43 of the CA 1994 in order to successfully claim share rectification. SAB has failed to show that any default had been made by CBL under section 43. This is because no specific complaints and/or claims had been made by SAB against CBL. So, it is clear that there was no cause of action under section 43 against CBL.

28. Mr Sattar submitted that SAB consistently alleged that he was the owner of the Disputed Shares and thereby, a shareholder in CBL. However, as this Court finds, there is no credible evidence had been produced by SAB to show that he was the legal owner of the Disputed Shares at any stage so' that his name should appear in the share register. SAB alleged that SAC entered into an understanding with SAB and transferred the Disputed Shares. This, according to CBL, was incorrect since the Disputed Shares were never transferred to SAB in accordance with section 38(3) of the CA 1994, which is a clear violation of law. Although SAB may have entered into an alleged understanding with SAC, the legal position is that the same has no legal sanction and does not bind CBL and/or any third party without notice. Mr Sattar aptly submitted that the share transfers must take place through duly executed share transfer instruments and share certificates. Mr Sattar referred to the case of Haque Brothers vs Shamsul Haque, 39 DLR 290, where it was held that:

"14. From the judgment of the Company judge, we find that the Company Judge on the facts of the present case found that there might be an arrangement between the brothers having no legal sanction. In this regards we may refer to section 34(3) of the Companies Act which says that the transfer of shares shall not be lawful without any instrument of transfer. Though transfer may be voluntary act of the parties but until an instrument is executed as contemplated under section 34(3) of the Companies Act, the legal title remains with the transferor ......"

29. CBL further submitted that SAB had never demanded or written to CBL that its share register be rectified in order to reflect the fact that SAB is the owner of the Disputed Shares. SAB never lodged any duly executed instruments of transfer to CBL, as required by s. 38(3) of the CA 1994. SAB's right to apply under section 43 would arise only if there has been a default on the part of CBL in registering SAB's name as a member in its share register. As no such instrument had been delivered by SAB to CBL, it is clear to this Court that CBL had not committed any default under section 43. This Court notes that the legal position had been rightly summarized in the case of Sm. Hemlata Saha v Stadmed Private Ltd And Ors, AIR 1965 Cal 436 where it was held by the Calcutta High Court that:

"17. An application under Section 155 [relating to rectification of share register] can be made by a party when the company has acted in violation of the terms and conditions laid down in that section. The applicant must satisfy the Court that the company has committed a breach of duty or a default as contemplated by that section. Unless therefore, there is evidence of a breach of duty or default, an application under section 155 cannot be sustained.

18. The petitioner's right to apply under section 155(1)(b) would arise only if there has been default on the part of the company in registering her name as a member in the Share Register of the company. But in this case, it cannot be said that the company has committed a default because the petitioner did not lodge with the company, an instrument of "transfer, without which the company has been forbidden by law to register a transfer. It cannot be said therefore, that the company is guilty of a default, which entitles the petitioner to move this court under section 155. Default implies an obligation to perform a duty and in this case it cannot be said that the company's duty to register the petitioner ever arose, because there was no instrument of transfer before it, upon which it could act and without which law forbids it to record a transfer. In this case, as no such instrument has been delivered by or on behalf of the petitioner to the company, the company has not committed a default under section 155(1)(b) of the Act. In that view of the matter, this application under section 155 is not maintainable."

30. CBL submitted that the present section 43 Application involves complicated and disputed questions of fact which cannot be decided in summary proceedings under section 43. It is clear from SAB's case that the present dispute is a civil dispute between SAB, BFIC and Hasan & Co. and involves issues of specific performance, disputed questions of facts relating to the alleged share sale agreement, loans granted by a financial institution, pledge of the Disputed Shares and, most importantly, SAB's title to the Disputed Shares and/or any right shares issued there against.

<u>31. Since it is evident that there is a clear dispute in relation to the title of the Disputed Shares which cannot be settled unless detailed investigation is pursued and evidence is taken, this Court finds that such disputed questions of fact cannot be settled in such proceedings under section 43 of the CA 1994. Section 43 is used to provide remedy in non-controversial matters where there is no need for detailed examination of complicated questions of fact and law, requiring extensive oral and documentary evidence. It cannot be inferred by this Court from section 43(3) that the remedy is not summary. In the case of Ellal Textile Mills Ltd. vs Md Abdul Awal, 38 DLR (AD) 26 this position was unambiguously confirmed by the Appellate Division of Bangladesh. The Appellate Division held:</u>

<u>"20. Summarizing the aforesaid principles it appears that section 38 (relating to share rectification) provides for summary jurisdiction and the Court will only entertain such discretion when there is no complicated question of title. But if any title is decided then appeal will lie thereto."</u>

32. In explaining the Companies Court's powers in relation to deciding the title of an aggrieved person's share, the Calcutta High Court, in Smt. Nupur Mitra vs Basubani Pvt. Ltd., (1999) 2 CALLT 264 HC at paragraph 73 referred to the decision of the Full Bench of the Delhi High Court in Ammonia Supply Corporation Private Limited vs Modern Plastic Containers Private Limited, 79 Comp. Cases 163:

"73. The object of section 155, in our view, is to provide remedy in non-controversial matters or in matters where a quick decision is necessary and can be rendered in order to obviate irreparable injury to a party. Section 155 is ordinarily not intended for settling controversies necessitating a regular investigation and in such cases the company court can decline to entertain petitions in exercise of its discretionary power and say that since serious disputes are involved, the proper forum for their adjudication is a civil court, section 155(3) only shows that questions relating to title can also be examined by the company court but that is also possible without detailed examination of complicated question of fact and law, requiring extensive oral and documentary evidence and it cannot be inferred from section 155(3) that the remedy is not summary. It would depend on the facts of each case..."

<u>33. More recently, in the case of Harbaksh Singh Batra vs Larsen and Toubro Ltd., (2010) 158 Com Cases 313 (CLB) at page 323, the Company Law Board refused share rectification on the ground that this provision is not intended for settling controversies necessitating a regular investigation on the title of the shares. If there are serious disputes involved, the proper forum for their adjudication is the civil court and not under summary proceedings. The Company Law Board held that:</u>

<u>"This provision is ordinarily not intended for settling controversies necessitating a regular investigation. If there are serious disputes involved, the proper forum for their adjudication is a civil court. The Company Law Board can examine the question relating to title without detailed examination of complicated questions of fact and law requiring extensive oral and documentary evidence ... In the present case the dispute is in respect of title and ownership of shares which needs extensive oral and documentary evidence, examination of witnesses to decide the said dispute. This is not possible in section 111 which is summary in nature, but can be decided by a competent civil court."</u>

<u>34. It is also clear from CBL's Affidavit-in-Opposition that the Disputed Shares had been transferred to bonafide third parties for value long before the section 43 application was filed and Mr Sattar has correctly submitted that it is an established position that applications under section 43 are not maintainable if third party rights have accrued and any rectification would lead to the interest of these third parties to be adversely prejudiced. This indeed is a well-established principle of company law and has been rightly re-iterated in the case of Re ISIS Factors plc, [2004] BCC 359 where the English Chancery Division (Companies Court) held:</u>

<u>"105. Given these circumstances, I am of the view that rectification of the ISIS Factors register (whether in exercise of the court's discretion under section 359(2) or as part of the working out of a decree of specific performance) would be to the manifest prejudice of LSB which purchased that control in ignorance of Mr Dulai's claims and on the footing that it was acquiring the whole of that company's issued share capital. On that further ground, therefore, I would have declined to grant the relief claimed."</u>

35. This position has been long established as is evident from the case of Smt. Soma Vati Devi Chand vs Krishna Sugar Mills Ltd. AIR 1966 PH 44, where the Court referred to Halsbury's Laws of England, Third Edition, Volume 6 at page 218, where it was stated that:

"The Court will not give substantive relief by way of rectification of the register on an interlocutory application in an action, nor will it rectify the register in the absence of third parties whose rights will be affected by the rectification."

<u>36. Since the Disputed Shares were transferred to BFIC in 2002 and SAB had modified the section 43 application seeking "rectification" of the share register of CBL in 2010, after 8 (eight) long years, it is CBL's case that such delay defeats a section 43 application. This Court finds that delay in applying for section 43 rectification is a standalone ground for refusing the same. In the case of Re ISIS Factors plc, the Chancery Division (Companies Court) held:</u>

<u>"By sitting back and doing nothing for seven years until the day arrived, if it ever should, when it suited him to enforce his rights, Mr Dulai was failing to display the need for promptitude which is ordinarily a requirement of someone seeking the grant in his favour of the court's discretion. That is certainly the case where specific performance is claimed. It is difficult to see why the position should be different merely because the claim is for relief under s.359. Delay of this length would without more have led me to refuse relief."</u>

37. In the case of Smt. Soma Vati Devi Chand vs Krishna Sugar Mills Ltd., the Court referred to the law in England in Halsbury's Laws of England, Third Edition, Volume 6, Page 218, where it was stated that:

"The application to rectify must be made promptly."

38. More recently, in the case of Harbaksh Singh Batra vs Larsen and Toubro Ltd, the Company Law Board refused share rectification on the ground of delay:

"A reasonable delay can be entertained but an inordinate delay of more than 11 years cannot be entertained that too without there being sufficient cause or reason. It unequivocally attracts the principles of laches and is hopelessly barred by the law of limitation. It is a settled principle that delay defeats equity. It is also well established principle that ignorance of law cannot be excused. Therefore, the petition is liable to be dismissed on this ground itself"

39. Lastly, in relation to SAB's alternative claim for damages against CBL, Mr Sattar submitted that since it has not committed any violation of section 43, it is clear that there is no cause of action against CBL. Hence, no claim for damages ought to be allowed against CBL. Also, damages in lieu of share rectification is not permitted as is clear from the obvious language of section 43(2), which should be given its plain ordinary meaning. CBL submitted that damages can only be awarded if rectification is allowed. Here as well, Mr Sattar's submissions merit favourable consideration by this Court. There is indeed a well-established position of such interconnectedness in law as confirmed in the case of Re Ottos Kopje Diamond Mines, Limited, [1893] 1 Ch. 618 at page 4, where Lindley 14J as part of the Court of Appeal held that:

"All I will say as to that order is, that I doubt whether there was any jurisdiction to make it, for it appears to me that the Court  has no jurisdiction under sect. 35 of the  Companies Act, 1862, to direct the company to pay damages except in cases  where an order is made for the rectification  of the register. I only make this remark because it must be borne in mind that  damages without rectification cannot be  obtained  by a summons under sect. 35 of the Act of 1862 instead of by an action at law "

40. In the case of Praga Tools Corporation Ltd. vs MR Patny, (1966) AIR 1968 AP 320, the Andhra High Court referred to the judgment of Re Ottos Kopje Diamond Mines, Limited and concluded that:

"11..... Where rectification is refused, there is no question of any damages being awarded by the company under that section ... It is, therefore clear that it is only after rectification that the question of awarding damages would arise."

41. In Ram Kishan, vs Kanwar Papers Private Ltd., 1990 (69) Com. Cas. 209. (HP) at page 220, the Himachal Pradesh High Court held that:

"The next question which arises is about the prayer made by these three applicants for being awarded damages on account of the wrong inclusion of their names in the register of members. It has been urged; with reference to the provision contained, in section 155(2) of the Act, that the respondent-company be directed to pay damages to the three applicants. When one looks at section 155(2L one finds that the court may direct the company to pay damages, if any, sustained by any party aggrieved, where it directs rectification of the register of members of the company. The language is suggestive of the fact that there should be a claim of sustenance of some damages by the party, in whose favour an order of rectification has been made, and actual proof of sustenance of such damages."

42. Based on the submissions put forward on behalf of the various Respondents and a consideration of the judicial authority discussed hereinabove, this Court finds that the Petitioner's claim in Company Matter No. 80 of 2006 must fail altogether.

Company Matter No. 35 of 2015

75. On 2-3-2015, the instant Company Matter was filed by SAB, under section 43 ("section 43") of the Companies Act 1994 (the "CA 1994"). The Respondent No. 1 is BFIC, the Respondent No. 2 is CBL, the Respondent No. 3 is DSE, the Respondent No. 4 is SAC, the Respondent No. 5 is ZH, the Respondent No. 6 is Registrar of Joint Stock Companies and Firms ("RJSCF") and the Respondent No. 7 is SEC.

76. In his section 43 application, SAB sought certain orders from this Court, which included the following:

(i) To direct BFIC to issue a NOC in respect of the 19,200 ordinary shares arising out of the Disputed Shares (the "Rights Shares") and all rights and bonus shares issued there against in the name of SAB;

(ii) To direct CBL to act upon the NOC and rectify its share register to enter the name of SAB in relation to the Rights Shares and all rights and bonus shares issued there against

(iii) To pass an order directing BFIC to pay damages of an amount of BDT 27,04,00,101.715 to SAB in case rectification is not possible for impracticability or for any other reason; and

(iv) Pending hearing of the section 43 application, a direction on BFIC and CBL that they should not enter into any transaction, deal with or transfer the Rights Shares.

77. As the Rights Shares were directly related to or was issued as a result of the underlying Disputed Shares, upon prayer of CBL and after hearing the parties at length, the instant section 43 application was heard analogously by this Companies Court with Company Matter No. 88 of 2006.

78. The relevant factual background, in short and as alleged by SAB, is that ZH took a loan (the "First Loan") from BFIC. In this connection, SAC pledged, as third party security for the First Loan, the Disputed Shares to BFIC. SAC delivered the signed share transfer forms relating to the Disputed Shares to BFIC in order to perfect the pledge. In the meantime, CBL issued the Rights Shares on a 1:2 ratio on 23-3-2002 and the same was credited in the name of BFIC, as the registered owner of the Disputed Shares. However, since the Disputed Shares were in the name of BFIC, SAB needed the NOC to transfer the Disputed Shares in its own name. BFIC submitted an Affidavit-in-Opposition and stated that SAB's statements in this section 43 application is different to the statements made in Company Matter No. 88 of 2006, even though it related to the same set of events and the same Disputed Shares. BFIC further stated that since the Disputed Shares were in the name of BFIC when the Rights Shares were issued, BFIC was entitled to receive the Right Shares in its own name free from any claim by SAB. BFIC claimed that the Disputed Shares were returned to the nominated representative of SAB, Md Shafiqul Islam, when the Second Loan was adjusted. 82. However, it is BFIC's main case that no person can legally have a claim over the Rights Shares, which were rightfully subscribed to by BFIC as a rights issue. The Right Shares were issued by CBL in accordance with the CA 1994 and the SEC (Rights Issue) Rules 2006 to BFIC, who was then the registered shareholder of the Disputed Shares, and after BFIC had legally paid the subscription money for it. The Rights Shares were never issued to SAB and SAB can never have any claim on the Rights Shares. Admittedly, the Disputed Shares, which were pledged, were returned to SAB. Even then, BFIC stated that the Disputed Shares were never wrongly held by BFIC, as originally they were received as security, and transferred upon failure of timely repayment of the First Loan. Accordingly, SAC could not have assigned the Disputed Shares to SAB. Contrary to SAB's allegations, BFIC never gave SAB any assurance as to the Right Shares. BFIC was the lawful owner of the Rights Shares and has never recognized SAB's right over these shares. The Right Shares were never pledged and, therefore, BFIC shall not return these shares or issue any NOC over the same.

83. BFIC also submitted that the Right Shares arising out of the Disputed Shares are already the subject matter of Company Matter No. 88 of 2006 and the decision of Company Matter No. 88 of 2006 would operate as res judicata on this section 43 application. Hence, this section 43 application is an abuse of process and is not legally maintainable.

84. On the other hand, CBL filed an Affidavit-in-Opposition clearly stating that SAB was never the owner of the Disputed Shares as per its records. As a result, CBL rightly issued the Rights Shares to BFIC against the Disputed Shares on 3042-2002. Also, there is no scope for BFIC to issue a NOC as the Rights Shares were transferred to third parties before the Company Matter No. 88 of 2006 and the instant section 43 application were initiated. As per CBL's records, the Rights Shares were transferred from BFIC to Laila Ali on 22-3-2004. Thereafter, the Rights Shares were transferred to bonafide third party purchasers, all before the filing of the instant section 43 application. CBL also stated that, at the time of these transfers, SAB never even complained and/or objected to CBL regarding the transfer of the Rights Shares. CBL also stated that, upon an order passed by SEC, the shares of CBL were to be treated as 'eligible securities' and cannot be traded on the DSE unless they are dematerialized. Therefore, CBL dematerialized all its shares. After dematerialization, shares have no specific share certificate numbers as opposed to paper shares. Therefore, it is not possible to identify specific shares using such numbers as they are now traded through the individual's beneficiary account.

85. It is also CBL's affirmative case that the Right Shares arising out of the Disputed Shares are already the subject matter of Company Matter No. 88 of 2006 and the decision of Company Matter No. 88 of 2006 would operate as res judicata on this section 43 application. Hence, this section 43 application is an abuse of process and is not legally maintainable.

86. It is noted that this Application, though confining itself to the Rights Issue, effectively addresses all lacunae in the Petitioner SAB's Case in Matter No. 88 of 2006 and seeks to clarify the "weakest link" in the 2006 case, i.e., BFICL's "ownership" of 38,400 shares as of 14-3-2002. It is argued that 14-3-2002 witnessed on "unauthorized conversion" taking place in violation of the very concept inherent in a "pledge" and section 176 of the Contract Act. SAB argues that his remedy lies in the tort of conversion that is available under a section 43 Application.

87. The submissions by SAB's legal Counsel Mr Akhtar Imam in Matter No. 35 have caused this Court to transfer its focus away from Hasan & Co. and concentrate on alleged wrongdoing on BFICL's part. Mr Akhtar Imam has sought to explain the "weakest link" in Matter No. 88 of 2016 thus: BFIC acted illegally on 14-3-2002 on the pledged shares without prior notice. The subsequent return of the 38,400 shares to the assignee Petitioner SAB will not be construed as in any way to be a waiver of entitlement to SAB's claim on unauthorized conversion, such entitlement is found/deemed to have accrued to SAB's predecessor-in-interest SAC at the material time and passed on to SAB and, according to Mr Imam, is found to be still alive. Nor can BFIC, by such line of argument, now claim the eventual return of said shares to SAB as a mitigating factor. This Court notes that Mr Akhtar Imam's submissions as above mark a shift in SAB's case in the sense of focusing on BFIC instead of Hasan & Co. That shift, this Court finds, is in a sense an admission of the weak case for intervention in section 43 citing lapses of Hasan & Co. Nor does this Court find a case against BFIC maintainable in the facts in the tort of conversion under the garb and guise of a section 43 Application as this.

88. Mr Akhtar Imam submits that it is not in dispute that the 38,400 shares were pledged with BFIC. BFIC itself acknowledged that the arrangement is a pledge (See Annexure C, D, I-2 and 1-3 at p. 46, 48, 70 and 72 of the Petition). Predicated on that understanding, Mr Imam has explained that a pledge can be created by handing over blank instrument of transfer and in this regard, the characterization by the contracting parties is a good indication to determine whether or not a transaction is a pledge (Sri Raja Kakarlapudi vs Anadhra Bank AIR 1960 AP 273 at para. 20). Here there is no reason to assume that BFIC used the word "pledge" in its letters dated 9-6-2002 and 4-8-2002 in the Share Deposit Memorandum, and the Sanction Letter dated 29-12-2002 by inadvertence and from the documents it is clear that parties (i.e. SAC, SAB and BFIC) throughout treated the transactions (both in the First Loan and the Second Loan) as one of pledge. Mr Imam has expanded further on his arguments by stressing that in case of pledge, unlike a sale, only "special rights" passes from the pledger (SAC or SAB) to the pledge (BFIC) and the "general property" remains with the pledger the owner of the goods pledged. Section 172 of the Contract Act 1872 ("the Contract Act") defined 'pledge' as the bailment of goods as security for payment of a debt or performance of a promise. The section also states that the bailor is called the 'pawnor' and the bailee is called the 'pawnee'. In MR Dhawan vs Madan Mohan, AIR 1969 Delhi 313, the Delhi High Court described the rights of pledger and pledgee at para. 10 as follows:

"The pawnee at no time becomes the owner of the goods pledged. He has only a right to retain the goods until his claim for the money advanced thereon has been satisfied, with a power to sell the goods pledged, after due notice in case of default by the pawner. It is only a special property in the goods pledged, which is acquired by the pawnee, leaving the general property intact with the pawner."

89. From the facts, it is noted that the First Loan was fully adjusted on 8-10-2002 and BFIC acknowledged the same vide its money receipt dated 8-10-2002 (Annexure- F at p. 53 of the Petition) and BFIC issued a no-dues certificate dated 18-12-2002 (Annexure-G at p. 56 of the Petition) to SAC where it is stated that 38,400 Shares were "delivered" to SAC. Therefore, as of 18-12-2002 (by when the First Loan was paid off), BFIC was treating the 38,400 Shares to be owned by SAC despite the fact that BFIC took ownership of these shares on 14-3-2002. There-fore, it is submitted that the during the tenure of the First Loan, no event of default occurred which would enable BFIC to trigger the provisions of the SAC Agreement and take 38,400 Shares in its name. More importantly, the actions of BFIC, as evidenced by its letters dated 9-6-2002 and 4-8-2002 (See Annexure C and D at p. 46 and 48 of the Petition) and 18-12-2002 (See Annexure G at p. 56 of the Petition) show that it never treated 38,400 Shares as its own despite the fact that these shares were in its name from 14-3-2002.

90. It is submitted that the above analysis is equally applicable when 38,400 Shares were pledged by the Petitioner for the Second Loan. During the tenure of the Second Loan, no event of default occurred which would enable BFIC to trigger the provisions of the SAB Agreement and take 38,400 Shares in its name. More importantly, the actions of BFIC, as evidenced by the SAB Agreement the Petitioner's POA and the Share Deposit Memorandum and BFIC's letter dated 19-4-2004 show that it never treated 38,400 Shares as its own despite the fact that these shares were in its name from 14-3-2002.

91. Therefore, it is submitted that BFIC never owned 38,400 Shares and, as evidenced by documents, never treated these 38,400 Shares as its own despite the fact that it arranged for these shares be transferred in its name on 14-3-2002.

<u>92. CBL has in response, however, aptly questioned the justification of such arguments placed through a section 43 Application as this. Mr Sattar has satisfactorily pleaded against such arguments being entertained in the present forum emphasizing that they instead are indicative of a civil dispute as to title. It is clear to this Court from the Application that the present dispute is in the nature of a civil dispute between SAB, SAC and BFIC and involves issues of specific performance, disputed questions of facts relating to the title of the Right Shares, alleged share sale agreement, loans granted by a financial institution and pledge of the Shares. It is this Court's view that such disputed questions of fact cannot be settled in a summary proceeding under section 43 of the CA 1994. In this regard this Court deems it pertinent to delve into relevant authority that have with precision set out both the parameters and the perimeter of this Court's statutory authority function and mandate under section 43 of the CA 1994.</u>

93. In the case of Abdur Rashid Chowdhury vs CA Hamid & Co., it was held that:

"The section gives the Court wide discretion to decide any matter relating to the rectification of a register of members of a company but such power would not mean iksm22  Court and decide each and every difference or dispute between , the members of a company. The jurisdiction of the court is no doubt of summary nature but unlimited for the pole purpose of rectification of the register."

94. In the case of Ellal Textile Mills Ltd. vs Md Abdul Awal, this position was unambiguously confirmed by the Appellate Division of Bangladesh. The Appellate Division held:

"Summarizing the aforesaid principles it appears that section 38 (relating to share rectification) provides for summary jurisdiction and the Court will only entertain such discretion when there is no complicated question of title, But if any title is decided then appeal will lie thereto."

95. In case of Maheshwari Khetan Sugar Mills vs Ishwari Khetan Sugar Mills, it was held:

"The scope of section 155 of the Companies Act, 1956[relating to share rectification], is now beyond controversy. It is the settled view of most of the High Courts that the summary remedy provided by section 155 need not be availed or the Courts may decline to exercise the ,power under section 155 leaving it open to the aggrieved party to seek remedy before a regular court, where there exists a serious dispute relating to the title a party to the proceeding. See Ramesh Chandra vs Jogini Mohan, AIR 1920 Cal 789; Mahadeo Lal vs New Darjeeling Union Tea Co. Ltd., AIR 1952 Cal 58; Jayshree Shantaram vs Rajkamal Kalamandir Private Ltd., AIR 1960 Born 136; Mohideen Pichal vs Tinnevelly Mills Co. Ltd., AIR 1928 Mad 571; Devakumar Mishara vs Rupak Ltd., AIR 1955 Pat 486; Laxminarayan Bhayyaa vs Praga Tools Corporation Ltd., AIR 1953 Hyd 126 and In re Ruby Consolidated Mining Co., (1874) 19 Ch. A. 664"

96. This position was further made clear in the case of Smt. Soma Vati Devi Chand vs Krishna Sugar Mills Ltd., where it was held by the Punjab-Haryana High Court that:

"Section 155 of the Companies Act deals with the power of Court to rectify the register of members and provides that if the name of any person is without sufficient cause, entered in the register of members of a company, or after having been entered in the register, is, without sufficient cause, omitted therefrom; or default is made, or delay takes place in making the necessary entry on the register, the person aggrieved, or any member of the Company, may apply to the Court for rectification of the register. This section corresponds to section 38 of the Companies Act, 1913 and section 116 of the English Companies Act, 1948. Although the power conferred by the section on Courts is very wide, the law seems to be well settled that the remedy provided by the section is summary and can be invoked in non-controversial matter requiring decision.  The provisions are not meant to be used for deciding disputes, necessitating investigation. Where the dispute is of a complicated nature and there is controversy under several heads and a regular investigation is necessary, the section ought not to be allowed to be used and the party concerned should be directed to proceed by way regular suit "

97. In explaining the Court's power in relation to deciding the title of an aggrieved person's share, the Calcutta High Court, in Smt. Nupur Mitra, vs Basubani, Pvt. Ltd., referred to the Full Bench decision of the Delhi High Court in Ammonia Supply Corporation Private Limited vs Modern Plastic Containers Private Limited, 79 Comp. Cases 163:

"The object of section 155, in our view is to provide remedy in non-controversial matters or in matters where a quick decision is necessary and can be rendered in order to obviate irreparable injury to a party. Section 155 is ordinarily not intended  for settling controversies necessitating a  regular investigation and in such cases the company court can decline to entertain petitions in exercise of its discretionary power and say that since serious disputes  are involved, the power forum for their  adjudication is a civil court, section 155(3)  only shows that questions relating to title can also be examined by the company court but that is also possible without detailed examination of complicated question of fact and law, requiring extensive oral and  documentary evidence and it cannot be  inferred from section 155(3) that the remedy is not summary. It would depend on the fact of each case"

<u>98. More recently, in the case of Harbaksh Singh Batra vs Larsen and Toubro Ltd., the Company Law Board refused share rectification on the ground that this provision is not intended for settling controversies necessitating a regular investigation on the title of shares. If there are serious disputes involved, the proper forum for their adjudication is the civil court and not under summary proceedings. The Company Law Board held that:</u>

<u>"This provision is ordinarily not intended for settling controversies necessitating a regular investigation. If there are serious disputes involved, the proper forum for their adjudication is a civil court.  The Company law Board can examine the question relating to title without detailed examination of complicated questions of fact and law requiring extensive oral and documentary evidence. In the present case the dispute is in respect of title and ownership of shares which needs extensive oral and documentary evidence, examination of witnesses to decide the said dispute. This is not possible in section 111 which is summary in nature, but can be decided by a competent civil court."</u>

99. Given the above circumstances, this Court finds that this Matter as well does not permit of substantive consideration by invocation of section 43 of the CA, 1994.

100. In the result, for reasons as above explained and substantiated all four section 43 Applications stand dismissed. Consequentially, any ad interim Order(s) issued initially or thereafter are, hereby, necessarily recalled and vacated.

There is no Order as to costs.
